title: A Giant Cosmic 'Fart' Is Making a Zombie Star Flash
summary:
Imagine a zombie star — the crushed leftover of an exploded sun — spinning in space. Every 11 minutes, it shoots a beam of X-rays toward Earth. But sometimes it flashes much brighter. Why? Scientists finally know: it's flying through a giant cosmic fart.

The zombie is a neutron star called GX 301-2. It's about 12 miles wide but has the same mass as our Sun. Its partner is a huge blue star named Wray 977, about 60 times bigger than the Sun. Wray 977 blasts out a plume of hot gas at 335,000 mph. That's the cosmic fart.

When GX 301-2 swings through the plume, gas piles onto its surface. When enough piles up — BOOM! — it erupts in bright X-rays.

Scientists used a space telescope called XRISM to watch this happen. It's the first time anyone has seen this kind of gas hitting a dead star. "We've never before seen clear indications of wind plasma falling onto a compact object," said lead researcher Roi Rahin.

Studying this weird pair helps us understand how extreme objects in space interact. And it all started with a fart.
why_it_matters: Studying these faraway 'zombie stars' shows that the same rules of energy and matter work everywhere, and a funny nickname can make hard science easier to remember.

background_read: A neutron star is what is left after a huge star explodes. It squeezes more stuff than our Sun into a ball only a few miles wide, which makes it incredibly heavy for its tiny size.
XRISM (a space telescope built by Japan with help from other space agencies) watches X-rays coming from space, and that is how scientists spotted this flashing.
Big blue stars like Wray 977 are much larger and hotter than our Sun, and they blow out powerful streams of hot gas into space.
Article_Structure: WHO: Astronomers studying a neutron star called GX 301-2 and its partner, the huge blue star Wray 977.
WHAT: They discovered that the zombie star flashes much brighter when it swings through a plume of hot gas — a cosmic 'fart' — from its partner.
WHERE: Deep in space, far from Earth, watched with a space telescope called XRISM.
WHY: To understand what happens when gas from a living star lands on a dead star, and how extreme objects in space affect each other.

perspectives.description: They are thrilled to see, for the first time, gas from a living star falling onto a dead one and making it flash brighter.
They say the funny 'fart' nickname is fine for a headline, but the real value is learning how extreme objects in space feed and change each other.
For people who love space, the story is a reminder that the universe is full of strange pairs of stars doing surprising things.
